pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.identification_seasoned: Tiny slender insects rasping silvery streaks and flecks into the leaf necks and folds; heavy feeding reduces bulb size and invites disease.
pests.identification_beginner: Very small insects that leave silvery streaks and specks on the leaves, often down in the crease where leaves meet. Bad infestations shrink the bulbs.
pests.cause_seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) build through warm, dry spells, sheltering in the leaf axils where sprays miss them.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny insect called onion thrips. It multiplies fast in warm, dry weather and hides in the tight folds of the leaves.
pests.management_seasoned: Clear volunteer onions and crop debris at the end of the season, since thrips overwinter in onion material left on the surface, and keep the bed away from small grains, alfalfa or clover, which shed thrips into onions when they dry down or are cut. Hold nitrogen to adequate rather than heavy, since excess promotes thrips, and keep plants well watered: vigor buys tolerance of the feeding rather than fewer thrips. A hard spray of water into the leaf folds knocks a light infestation back, straw mulch on the bed has been shown to reduce populations, and minute pirate bugs and lacewings help where broad-spectrum sprays are avoided. Treat persistent outbreaks per local extension guidance.
pests.management_beginner: At the end of the season pull any onions left in the bed and clear the debris, because that is where thrips spend the winter, and do not put onions right beside a grain, alfalfa or clover patch, which sends thrips into them when it dries or is cut. Go easy on nitrogen, which makes thrips worse, and keep the plants well watered so they can shrug off the feeding. Wash light infestations off with a hard spray from the hose aimed down into the leaf folds, and a straw mulch on the bed helps hold numbers down. For heavy infestations, ask your local extension office what to use.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.identification_seasoned: Wilting, yellowing seedlings and rotting bulbs riddled by small white larvae; stand loss is worst in cool, wet springs.
pests.identification_beginner: Young plants wilt and yellow, and bulbs rot with small white grubs inside. Worst in cool, wet spring weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the onion maggot fly (Delia antiqua), which lays at the base of the plant; the pupae overwinter in the soil around last season's onions, and cull piles and volunteer onions keep the fly going between crops. Rotting organic matter and spring manure draw egg-laying, and the first flight arrives with the cool, wet weather of mid-spring.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (maggots) of a small fly that lays its eggs at the base of onion plants. It spends the winter in the soil where onions grew the year before, and old bulbs and rotting garden waste draw it in.
pests.management_seasoned: Rotate off ground that carried alliums last season and site new plantings away from it and from any cull pile, remove culls and volunteer onions, keep spring manure and green manure out of the bed, and cover seedlings or sets with row cover sealed at the edges from planting, before the spring flight, on ground that did not carry alliums last year. Delaying planting until the first flight has passed reduces damage where the season allows.
pests.management_beginner: Do not plant onions where onions or their relatives grew last year, clear out old bulbs and any onion volunteers, keep fresh manure out of the bed in spring, and cover the young plants with row-cover fabric from planting day so the fly cannot lay eggs on them. Do not cover a bed that grew alliums last year, or you seal the emerging flies in with the crop.

diseases.name: Botrytis neck rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: A soft, sunken rot starting at the neck in storage, often with gray mold; white-skinned and immature or poorly cured bulbs are most susceptible.
diseases.identification_beginner: Onions go soft and rotten at the neck after harvest, sometimes with gray mold. It mostly hits white onions and bulbs that were not dried well.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis infection of immature or insufficiently cured necks; excess nitrogen and bent-over green tops worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A mold that gets into the neck of onions that were harvested too green or not dried properly. Too much fertilizer and bending the tops down make it worse.
diseases.management_seasoned: Let tops mature naturally, do not knock down green tops to force bulbing, cure thoroughly, and store cool and dry.
diseases.management_beginner: Let the tops fall on their own, do not bend them over, dry (cure) the onions well, and store them somewhere cool and dry.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.identification_seasoned: Browning, decay, and pink-to-brown discoloration at the basal plate, with roots dying back; bulbs rot from the bottom in the field and in storage.
diseases.identification_beginner: The bottom of the bulb (the root end) turns brown and rots, and the roots die. The bulb decays from the base.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Fusarium that persists for years and is favored by warm soil; wounds and maggot damage open the door.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that stays in the ground for years and likes warm soil. Injuries and insect damage let it in.
diseases.management_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties where available, rotate out of alliums for several years, and avoid wounding bulbs.
diseases.management_beginner: Pick resistant varieties if you can, do not grow onions in the same spot for several years, and handle the bulbs gently so they are not injured.

diseases.name: Pink root
diseases.identification_seasoned: Roots turn pink then red and shrivel, stunting plants and shrinking bulbs; common where alliums are grown repeatedly and in warm soils.
diseases.identification_beginner: The roots turn pink, then red, then shrivel up. Plants stay small and make small bulbs. Common when onions are grown in the same place often.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne fungus (Setophoma terrestris, long known as Phoma terrestris) that penetrates onion roots directly without a wound, builds up with every onion crop on the same ground, and is most active at soil temperatures of 75 to 85°F; weak or stressed plants are the most susceptible, and heavy, poorly drained soil makes it worse.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil fungus that builds up when onions and their relatives are grown in the same ground year after year. Stressed plants get it worst.
diseases.management_seasoned: Resistant varieties are the best control, so ask your seed supplier which ones hold up locally, since resistance varies with the strain. Rotate off allium ground for three to six years, understanding that rotation reduces the disease rather than clearing it, because the fungus persists in soil for years. Keep plants vigorous with steady water and fertility, and improve drainage on heavy ground.
diseases.management_beginner: Choose a variety sold as resistant to pink root if you can, and ask your seed supplier which ones do well in your area. Give onions a bed that has not grown onions or their relatives for several years, keep them watered and fed so the roots stay strong, and improve drainage where the soil stays wet. Rotation helps but does not clear the fungus, which lasts in the soil for years.
